cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 1(a): Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. On 3 February 2026 the European Parliament and the Council adopt Regulation (EU) 2026/207 on the registration of cargo bikes (fictional). It is published in the Official Journal on 10 February 2026 and states that it applies from 1 September 2026. The existing registration law of Member State Ardenia contains different rules. The Ardenian Minister of Transport declares: 'Until our parliament has transposed the regulation into an Ardenian act, our authorities will continue to apply the Ardenian registration law.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. A regulation is directly applicable: from 1 September 2026 it applies in Ardenia as it stands, without any national transposition, and conflicting Ardenian law must be disapplied.
• Rule: a regulation has general application, is binding in its entirety and is directly applicable in all Member States (Art 288(2) TFEU). It enters into force on the date it specifies or on the 20th day after publication (Art 297(1) TFEU), and it may fix a later date of application.
• Direct applicability: entry into force and application do not depend on any national act of reception. Member States may not re-enact a regulation in a way that conceals its EU nature (Variola, 34/73). National measures are allowed only where the regulation requires them, e.g. to designate authorities or lay down penalties (Art 291(1) TFEU).
• Application: from 1 September 2026 the Ardenian authorities, not only the courts, must apply the regulation and set aside the conflicting law (Simmenthal, 106/77; Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88). Ardenia should repeal that law for the sake of legal certainty, but the regulation's application does not depend on it.
Codex: Art 288(2), 291(1), 297(1) TFEU · not in the codex: Variola (34/73), Simmenthal (106/77), Fratelli Costanzo (103/88).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 1(b): Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. Directive (EU) 2025/1104 on noise emissions of garden equipment (fictional) had to be transposed by 1 June 2026. Member State Brenland 'transposes' it by an internal circular of its Ministry of the Environment, which instructs the regional authorities to apply the directive's noise limits when approving equipment. The circular is not published and the Minister can amend it at any time. Statement of the Brenland government: 'Since Art 288(3) TFEU leaves the choice of form and methods to the national authorities, Brenland has fulfilled its obligation.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. The freedom of form and methods does not extend to non-binding, unpublished administrative practice. Brenland has not transposed the directive and is in breach of Art 288(3) TFEU and Art 4(3) TEU.
• Rule: a directive binds as to the result and leaves the choice of form and methods to the Member State (Art 288(3) TFEU). But the form chosen must have unquestionable binding force and the clarity, precision and publicity that legal certainty requires, so that individuals can ascertain their rights and obligations and rely on them before the courts.
• Case law: mere administrative practices, which the administration can alter at will and which are not adequately publicised, are not proper transposition (Commission v Belgium, 102/79). Nor is an administrative circular whose binding force towards third parties and the courts is not established (Commission v Germany, C-361/88, TA Luft).
• Application: an unpublished circular that the Minister can change at any time fails both tests, so there has been no transposition since 1 June 2026. Consequences: an infringement action (Art 258 TFEU), vertical direct effect of sufficiently precise provisions, consistent interpretation, and possibly state liability.
Codex: Art 288(3), 258 TFEU; Art 4(3) TEU · not in the codex: Commission v Belgium (102/79), Commission v Germany (C-361/88).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 1(c): Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. Directive X (fictional) requires Member States to grant consumers compensation for delayed cross-border parcel deliveries. The Commission then adopts a Recommendation on how such delays should be calculated. In a dispute before a court of Member State Cordania between consumer Cora and parcel company Swiftpak, Cora relies on the Recommendation to interpret the Cordanian act transposing Directive X. Statement: 'A recommendation is not binding (Art 288(5) TFEU), so the Cordanian court may simply ignore it; Swiftpak can, however, bring an action for annulment against it.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No, on both counts. The court may not simply ignore the Recommendation (Grimaldi), and Swiftpak cannot have it annulled, because it produces no binding legal effects.
• Rule: recommendations have no binding force (Art 288(5) TFEU). But national courts are bound to take them into consideration when deciding disputes, in particular where they cast light on the interpretation of national measures implementing EU law or supplement binding EU provisions (Grimaldi, C-322/88).
• Application: the Recommendation explains how the compensation required by Directive X is to be calculated. The Cordanian court must therefore take it into account when interpreting the transposing act. It is not bound to follow it, but it may not disregard it.
• Annulment: Art 263(1) TFEU expressly excludes recommendations, and only acts intended to produce binding legal effects can be challenged (Belgium v Commission, C-16/16 P). The court may, however, refer questions on the Recommendation to the CJEU under Art 267(1)(b) TFEU, which covers all acts of the institutions, binding or not.
Codex: Art 288(5), 263(1), 267(1)(b) TFEU · not in the codex: Grimaldi (C-322/88), Belgium v Commission (C-16/16 P).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 1(d): Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. A Council decision (fictional) addressed to Member State Dorvania requires it to abolish, by 1 January 2026, a 'transit charge' that Dorvania levies only on lorries registered in other Member States. Dorvania continues to levy the charge. The haulier Vela Trans pays under protest and sues the Dorvanian tax office for repayment of the charges levied since 1 January 2026. Statement of the tax office: 'Vela Trans cannot rely on the decision, because under Art 288(4) TFEU a decision which specifies those to whom it is addressed is binding only on them.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. 'Binding only on the addressee' means that the decision binds Dorvania. An individual may invoke a clear, precise and unconditional obligation it imposes against that State (vertical direct effect, Grad), though not against a private party.
• Rule: a decision that specifies its addressees is binding in its entirety only on them (Art 288(4) TFEU). But excluding in principle the possibility for those concerned to invoke the obligation it imposes on the Member State would be incompatible with that binding effect and would weaken its effet utile. Art 267 TFEU, moreover, allows references on all acts of the institutions (Grad, 9/70).
• Conditions: the obligation must be clear, precise and unconditional, and the deadline for compliance must have expired. It cannot be relied on against another individual (Carp, C-80/06).
• Application: the duty to abolish one specific charge by 1 January 2026 is clear and unconditional, the deadline has passed, and the tax office is part of the State to which the decision is addressed. Vela Trans can therefore claim repayment of the charges levied since that date, under national procedural rules that respect equivalence and effectiveness (Rewe, 33/76).
Codex: Art 288(4), 267 TFEU · not in the codex: Grad (9/70), Carp (C-80/06), Rewe (33/76).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 2(a): Regulation (EU) 2026/518 on a digital product passport for textiles (fictional) was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure on the basis of Art 114 TFEU. Art 2 limits its scope to clothing and household textiles and expressly excludes footwear and leather goods. Art 9 empowers the Commission 'to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 20 to amend Annex III (information to be contained in the passport) in order to take account of technical progress'. Art 20 confers that power for five years and provides that a delegated act enters into force only if neither the Parliament nor the Council objects within two months of notification, a period that can be extended by two months. Art 14 provides: 'The Commission shall, by means of implementing acts, lay down the uniform technical format of the data carrier (QR code) and the interoperability requirements. Those implementing acts shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 21(2)' (which refers to Art 5 of Regulation 182/2011). Explain the legal nature of the acts the Commission may adopt under Art 9 and under Art 14, how they differ, and who controls them. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Art 9 confers a delegated power (Art 290 TFEU) to amend non-essential elements, controlled by the Parliament and the Council. Art 14 confers an implementing power (Art 291 TFEU) to lay down uniform conditions for implementation, controlled by the Member States through comitology.
• Common ground: both are non-legislative acts of the Commission ('tertiary law'). Both rank below the basic regulation and are unlawful if they depart from it. Their titles must contain the word 'delegated' or 'implementing' (Art 290(3), 291(4) TFEU).
• Art 9, delegated act: a legislative act may delegate the power to supplement or amend non-essential elements of it. The objectives, content, scope and duration of the delegation must be explicit (here: Annex III, technical progress, five years), and essential elements stay with the legislature (Art 290(1)). Control: the EP (by a majority of its component members) or the Council (by QMV) may revoke the delegation or object, in which case the act cannot enter into force (Art 290(2)).
• Art 14, implementing act: implementation is primarily a task of the Member States (Art 291(1)). Where uniform conditions are needed, such as one QR format for the whole internal market, the Commission receives implementing powers (Art 291(2)). Control: committees of Member State representatives under Regulation 182/2011 (Art 291(3)), here under the examination procedure (Art 5). The EP and the Council have only a non-binding right of scrutiny (Art 11).
• Delimitation: a delegated act changes or adds to the content of the basic act. An implementing act only gives effect to it and may neither amend nor supplement it (C-88/14). The Court reviews the legislature's choice between the two only for manifest error (Biocides, C-427/12).
Codex: Art 290, 291 TFEU · not in the codex: Regulation 182/2011 (Art 5, 11), Commission v Parliament and Council (C-88/14), Biocides (C-427/12).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 2(b): Regulation (EU) 2026/518 on a digital product passport for textiles (fictional), adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure, limits its scope in Art 2 to clothing and household textiles and expressly excludes footwear and leather goods. Art 9 empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts 'to amend Annex III (information to be contained in the passport) in order to take account of technical progress'. In a delegated act based on Art 9, the Commission adds to Annex III two new information items that new fibre-scanning technology has made it possible to record. In the same act it amends Art 2 so that the regulation also applies to footwear and leather goods. Is this lawful, and how can it be challenged? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: The amendment of Annex III is covered by the delegation. Extending the scope to footwear and leather goods is not: it exceeds the delegated power (and very probably concerns an essential element), so that part of the act is unlawful and can be annulled.
• Rule: a delegated act may supplement or amend only the non-essential elements that the legislative act explicitly delegates (Art 290(1) TFEU). Essential elements, meaning political choices that require conflicting interests to be weighed, are reserved to the legislature (Parliament v Council, C-355/10).
• Application: Art 9 covers only Annex III, and only 'to take account of technical progress', which the two new items do. The scope in Art 2, with its deliberate exclusion of footwear and leather goods, is a choice made by the legislature and lies outside the delegation.
• Remedies: the EP or the Council may object within the objection period or revoke the delegation (Art 290(2)). A Member State, the EP or the Council may bring an action for annulment within two months (Art 263(2), (6)); the Court may annul the severable Art 2 amendment alone (Art 264). Validity can also be contested before national courts, but only the CJEU can declare the act invalid, so a court with doubts must refer (Art 267; Foto-Frost, 314/85).
Codex: Art 290, 263, 264, 267 TFEU · not in the codex: Parliament v Council (C-355/10), Foto-Frost (314/85).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 2(c): Regulation (EU) 2026/518 on a digital product passport for textiles (fictional), adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure, empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts. It provides that a delegated act enters into force only if neither the European Parliament nor the Council objects within two months of notification, extendable by two months. The Commission notifies a delegated act on 2 March 2026. On 28 April 2026 the Parliament, all of whose 720 seats are filled, votes on a resolution objecting to the act: 351 in favour, 290 against, 40 abstentions. The Council does not object. Can the delegated act enter into force? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes. The objection failed, because the Parliament can object only by a majority of its component members (361 of 720), and 351 votes are not enough. As the Council did not object either, the act enters into force when the objection period expires.
• Rule: a delegated act may enter into force only if neither the EP nor the Council objects within the period set by the basic act. The EP acts by a majority of its component members and the Council by QMV (Art 290(2) TFEU). This departs from the usual rule of a majority of the votes cast (Art 231 TFEU).
• Application: the act was notified on 2 March 2026, so the two-month period runs into early May 2026 unless it is extended, and the vote on 28 April is in time. But 351 is less than 361 (half of 720 plus one). The majority of the votes cast (351 to 290) is irrelevant, so abstentions and absences in effect count against the objection.
• Remaining options: the EP may revoke the delegation for the future (Art 290(2)(a), with the same majority). As a privileged applicant, it may also bring an action for annulment within two months (Art 263(2), (6) TFEU).
Codex: Art 231, 263, 290(2) TFEU · not in the codex: 720 seats for 2024–2029 (European Council Decision (EU) 2023/2061).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 2(d): Regulation (EU) 2026/518 on a digital product passport for textiles (fictional), adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure, provides in Art 14 that the Commission shall lay down, by means of implementing acts, the uniform technical format of the passport's data carrier (QR code) and the interoperability requirements, in accordance with the examination procedure (Art 5 of Regulation 182/2011). The Commission submits a draft implementing act to the committee of Member State representatives. 14 Member States vote against, 9 in favour and 4 abstain, so neither a qualified majority in favour nor one against is reached. The Commission wants to adopt the act anyway. Can it? What can it do instead? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. No opinion was delivered, but a simple majority of the committee's component members (14 of 27) opposed the draft, so the Commission may not adopt it (Art 5(4) second subpara (c) of Regulation 182/2011). It may submit an amended draft to the same committee within two months, or refer the draft to the appeal committee within one month.
• Rule: in the examination procedure the committee votes by QMV under Art 16(4)–(5) TEU, i.e. at least 55% of the Member States (15 of 27) representing at least 65% of the population (Art 5(1)). A positive opinion means the Commission adopts the act (Art 5(2)); a negative opinion (a QMV against) means it may not adopt it (Art 5(3)). If no opinion is delivered, it MAY adopt the act (Art 5(4)), except where: (a) the act concerns taxation, financial services, the health or safety of humans, animals or plants, or definitive multilateral safeguard measures; (b) the basic act excludes adoption without an opinion; or (c) a simple majority of the committee's component members opposes it.
• Application: 9 votes in favour and 14 against are both below 15 Member States, so whatever the population figures, no opinion was delivered. A technical data format falls under none of the fields in (a), and the facts mention no clause under (b). But 14 of 27 is a simple majority against the draft, so exception (c) bars adoption.
• Next steps (Art 5(4) third subpara): the chair may submit an amended draft to the same committee within 2 months of the vote, or the draft to the appeal committee within 1 month. If the appeal committee delivers no opinion, the Commission may adopt the act; if it delivers a negative opinion, it may not (Art 6(3)). The EP and the Council may indicate that the draft exceeds the implementing powers, but this is not binding (Art 11).
Codex: Art 291(2)–(3) TFEU; Art 16(4)–(5) TEU · not in the codex: Regulation 182/2011, Art 5, 6, 11.

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 3(a): Regulation (EU) 2025/2290 on cross-border e-prescriptions (fictional), adopted on the basis of Art 114 TFEU, obliges every pharmacy in the Union in its Art 6 to dispense prescription medicines on an electronic prescription issued by a doctor in another Member State. § 7 of the Pharmacy Act (1998) of Member State Lumeria permits dispensing only on prescriptions issued by doctors registered in Lumeria. Pharmacist Petra dispenses a medicine in Lumeria on an e-prescription issued by a doctor in Slovenia. The regional health authority fines her under § 7, and she appeals to the Lumerian Administrative Court. Under the Lumerian Constitution, an ordinary court that considers a statute incompatible with higher-ranking law, including EU law, must suspend the proceedings and ask the Constitutional Court to annul the statute; until then it must apply the statute. Such proceedings take 14 months on average. Must the Administrative Court follow that procedure, or can it decide the case itself? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: It can and must decide the case itself. Every national court must set aside a conflicting statute immediately and of its own motion (Simmenthal). A rule obliging it to apply the statute until the Constitutional Court annuls it is incompatible with EU law (Melki).
• Starting point: Art 6 of the Regulation is directly applicable (Art 288(2) TFEU). Being clear, precise and unconditional, it is also directly effective, and Petra may invoke it as a defence against the fine. Under primacy (Costa v ENEL, 6/64; Declaration 17), conflicting national law of any rank must be disapplied.
• Simmenthal (106/77): every national court must apply EU law in its entirety and set aside any conflicting provision of national law, whether prior or subsequent. It must do so without requesting or awaiting the prior setting aside of that provision by legislative or other constitutional means.
• Priority constitutional review: it is compatible with EU law only if the ordinary courts remain free, at any stage, to refer questions to the CJEU, to grant interim protection, and to disapply the national provision afterwards (Melki and Abdeli, C-188/10 and C-189/10; for the Austrian Constitutional Court, A v B, C-112/13). The Lumerian rule requires § 7 to be applied until it is annulled. It fails this test, so it must itself be disapplied.
• Conclusion: the court disapplies § 7 and annuls the fine. If it is in doubt about the interpretation of Art 6, it may refer directly to the CJEU (Art 267(2) TFEU); a court of last instance must refer (Art 267(3)) unless the answer is obvious or already settled (CILFIT, 283/81).
Codex: Art 288(2), 267 TFEU; Declaration 17 · not in the codex: Costa v ENEL (6/64), Simmenthal (106/77), Melki and Abdeli (C-188/10), A v B (C-112/13), CILFIT (283/81).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 3(b): Art 6 of Regulation (EU) 2025/2290 on cross-border e-prescriptions (fictional) obliges every pharmacy in the Union to dispense medicines on e-prescriptions issued by doctors in other Member States. § 7 of the Pharmacy Act of Member State Lumeria permits dispensing only on prescriptions from doctors registered in Lumeria. The Lumerian Administrative Court disapplies § 7 because it conflicts with the Regulation, and annuls a fine imposed on pharmacist Petra. The Lumerian Ministry of Health then announces: '§ 7 has been declared void by the court and has therefore disappeared from Lumerian law; there is no need to amend the Pharmacy Act.' Do you agree? (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No. Primacy only means that § 7 is disapplied where it conflicts with EU law. It remains valid national law, and Lumeria must still amend it.
• Primacy is a conflict rule, not a nullity rule. Incompatibility with EU law does not make the national rule non-existent; the court must disapply it (IN.CO.GE.'90, C-10/97 to C-22/97). The judgment binds only the parties, and § 7 still governs situations outside the scope of EU law, e.g. prescriptions from doctors in third countries.
• However, keeping an incompatible statute unchanged creates an ambiguous state of affairs and legal uncertainty, which is itself a breach of EU law, here of the Regulation and of Art 4(3) TEU (Commission v France, 167/73, French Merchant Seamen). Lumeria must adapt § 7. Otherwise the Commission may bring an infringement action (Art 258 TFEU).
Codex: Art 4(3) TEU; Art 258 TFEU · not in the codex: IN.CO.GE.'90 (C-10/97), Commission v France (167/73).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 3(c): Regulation (EU) 2025/2290 on cross-border e-prescriptions (fictional), adopted on the basis of Art 114 TFEU, obliges every pharmacy in the Union to dispense medicines on e-prescriptions issued by doctors in other Member States. A group of MPs of Member State Lumeria challenges the Regulation before the Lumerian Constitutional Court. Without making a preliminary reference, the Constitutional Court rules that the Regulation is 'not applicable in Lumeria'. It gives two reasons: (i) under Art 168(7) TFEU the organisation of health services and pharmacies is reserved to the Member States, so the Union acted ultra vires; (ii) the self-administration of the pharmacists' profession is part of Lumeria's constitutional identity. Assess the ruling from the perspective of the Court of Justice, and explain the doctrines of 'constitutional reservation' on which national constitutional courts rely. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: For the CJEU the ruling infringes EU law. Only the CJEU can declare an EU act invalid or ultra vires, and the scope of national identity (Art 4(2) TEU) is a question of EU law that must be referred under Art 267 TFEU. National constitutional courts claim a residual power of fundamental-rights, ultra vires and identity review, but even by their own (German) standards only after a reference.
• CJEU view: any EU law prevails over any national law, including the constitution (Costa v ENEL, 6/64; Internationale Handelsgesellschaft, 11/70). The validity of EU acts, including the question of competence (Art 5(2) TEU, Art 168(7) TFEU), is for the CJEU alone (Art 263, 267 TFEU). National courts may not declare EU acts invalid (Foto-Frost, 314/85), and a constitutional court that considers an EU act contrary to national identity must stay the proceedings and refer (RS, C-430/21). In Commission v Poland (C-448/23, 18 December 2025) the Court confirmed that national courts may not rule unilaterally and definitively on the limits of Union competences; such doubts must be referred under Art 267.
• Consequences: ordinary Lumerian courts must still apply the Regulation and disregard the ruling (RS). The ruling is attributable to Lumeria, so the Commission may bring an infringement action (Art 258 TFEU). It did so against Poland (C-448/23), and after PSPP it opened proceedings against Germany (2021, closed after German assurances).
• National view (integration-proof core): primacy is accepted on the basis of the national constitution and only within the powers conferred. The German model has three strands. Fundamental-rights reservation: Solange I (1974), suspended by Solange II (1986). Ultra vires review: asserted in Maastricht (1993); Honeywell (2010) limits it to a manifest, structurally significant excess and requires a prior reference; first applied in PSPP (2020) after Weiss (C-493/17). Identity review: Lisbon (2009), based on Art 79(3) Basic Law and echoed by Art 4(2) TEU. Austria, Czechia, Denmark, France, Italy and Spain set similar limits.
• Application: the Lumerian court invoked ultra vires (i) and identity (ii) without referring, so it fails even the Honeywell test. Any excess of competence is at least not manifest, since harmonisation under Art 114 may affect national health systems (cf. Art 11 of Directive 2011/24 on recognising prescriptions issued in another Member State).
Codex: Art 4(2), 5(2) TEU; Art 114, 168(7), 258, 263, 267 TFEU · not in the codex: Costa v ENEL (6/64), Internationale Handelsgesellschaft (11/70), Foto-Frost (314/85), RS (C-430/21), Commission v Poland (C-448/23), Weiss (C-493/17), BVerfG Solange I/II, Maastricht, Lisbon, Honeywell, PSPP.

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 4(a) (case exercise): Directive (EU) 2024/1690 on night work in hospitals and emergency medical services (fictional) was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure and had to be transposed by 1 March 2026. Art 3: 'Member States shall ensure that workers who perform night work (22:00–06:00) in hospitals or emergency medical services receive from their employer an allowance of at least 25% of their basic hourly wage for every hour of night work.' Art 7: 'Member States shall ensure that, where an employer is insolvent, outstanding allowances under Article 3 are paid by a guarantee institution. Member States shall lay down the organisation and financing of that institution and may limit its liability to the allowances for the last three months before the onset of insolvency.' Assume that the Directive is valid. Valdoria, an EU Member State, has adopted no transposition measures. § 12 of the Valdorian Working Time Act (1994) provides: 'Night work shall be compensated in an appropriate manner'; the Valdorian courts have consistently read this as an allowance of 10%. Anna is a night nurse at Medicor GmbH, a hospital company owned by a private investment fund. Like every hospital, Medicor holds an operating licence and is supervised by the Valdorian Ministry of Health. Since 1 March 2026 Medicor has paid Anna a night allowance of only 10%. Anna sues Medicor before the Valdorian labour court for the difference up to 25%, relying on Art 3 of the Directive. Advise Anna. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Anna cannot rely on Art 3 against Medicor. Art 3 meets the conditions for direct effect and the deadline has passed, but a directive cannot of itself impose obligations on a private party, and Medicor is not an emanation of the State. She must rely on consistent interpretation of § 12 or, failing that, on state liability.
• Preliminary point: validity is assumed. (In reality a rule fixing pay levels would be open to challenge because Art 153(5) TFEU excludes pay, cf. Denmark v Parliament and Council, C-19/23; but only the CJEU could declare the Directive invalid: Foto-Frost, 314/85.)
• Step 1, the provision: it must be clear, precise and unconditional (Van Gend en Loos, 26/62). Art 3 names the beneficiaries (night workers in hospitals and emergency services), the debtor (the employer) and the content (at least 25% for every night hour between 22:00 and 06:00). The freedom to grant more does not make the minimum conditional. Met.
• Step 2, the category: a directive binds only as to the result (Art 288(3) TFEU), and the rule is that it has no direct effect. The exception is vertical direct effect, once the transposition deadline has expired and the State has failed to transpose or has transposed incorrectly (Van Duyn, 41/74; Ratti, 148/78). Met: the deadline was 1 March 2026 and nothing was transposed. The rationale is estoppel and effet utile.
• Step 3, the relationship: Anna against Medicor is horizontal. A directive cannot be relied on as such against a private party (Marshall I, 152/84; Faccini Dori, C-91/92; Smith, C-122/17): it is addressed only to Member States, the private party is not at fault, legal certainty requires it, and the distinction between regulations and directives would otherwise vanish. Medicor is not an emanation of the State: it is privately owned, and a licence and general supervision amount neither to State control nor to special powers (Foster, C-188/89; Farrell, C-413/15).
• No primary-law route: Art 31(2) of the Charter (working hours, rest periods, paid annual leave) can apply between private parties (Bauer, C-569/16), but it does not cover night-pay supplements. No general principle of EU law guarantees them either, unlike the prohibition of age discrimination (Mangold, C-144/04; Kücükdeveci, C-555/07).
• Conclusion: Anna has no claim on the Directive itself against Medicor. Her next routes are consistent interpretation of the open term 'appropriate' in § 12 (Von Colson, 14/83; Marleasing, C-106/89), which should give her the 25%, and, if that fails, Francovich damages from Valdoria.
Codex: Art 153(5), 288(3) TFEU; Art 31(2) Charter · not in the codex: Van Gend en Loos (26/62), Van Duyn (41/74), Ratti (148/78), Marshall I (152/84), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Smith (C-122/17), Foster (C-188/89), Farrell (C-413/15), Bauer (C-569/16), Mangold (C-144/04), Kücükdeveci (C-555/07), Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), Foto-Frost (314/85), Denmark v Parliament and Council (C-19/23).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 4(b) (case exercise, continued): Directive (EU) 2024/1690 on night work in hospitals and emergency medical services (fictional) had to be transposed by 1 March 2026. Its Art 3 obliges Member States to ensure that night workers (22:00–06:00) in hospitals or emergency medical services receive from their employer an allowance of at least 25% of their basic hourly wage for every hour of night work. Assume that the Directive is valid. Valdoria, an EU Member State, has adopted no transposition measures. § 12 of the Valdorian Working Time Act provides that night work 'shall be compensated in an appropriate manner', which the Valdorian courts read as 10%. Ben is a paramedic employed by Valdorian Rescue AG, a joint-stock company whose shares are wholly held by the Valdorian regions. The Rescue Services Act entrusts it with the exclusive operation of the public emergency ambulance service (emergency number 112). The Minister of Health fixes its tariffs and appoints its supervisory board, and its crews may use blue lights and enter private premises in emergencies. Since 1 March 2026 Rescue AG has paid Ben 10% for his night hours. Advise Ben. Does it matter that Rescue AG is a company governed by private law? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Ben can rely on Art 3 vertically against Rescue AG and claim 25% for the night hours he has worked since 1 March 2026, because Rescue AG is an emanation of the State. Its private-law form does not matter.
• Rule: a directly effective directive can be invoked against the State in any capacity, including as an employer (Marshall I, 152/84), and against all its organs, including decentralised authorities (Fratelli Costanzo, 103/88). 'The State' covers any body, whatever its legal form, that is subject to the authority or control of the State. It also covers a body to which the State has entrusted a task in the public interest and which has special powers for that purpose, beyond the normal rules between individuals (Foster, C-188/89). These criteria are alternative, not cumulative (Farrell, C-413/15).
• Application: Rescue AG is under State control, since the regions own it entirely and the Minister appoints its supervisory board and fixes its tariffs. It also performs a public task with special powers: the 112 service, which it runs exclusively by statute, blue lights, and entry into private premises. Both limbs are met, so the AG form is irrelevant.
• Consequence: Art 3 is clear, precise and unconditional, the deadline has expired and nothing was transposed. The labour court must apply Art 3 in Ben's favour and set aside the conflicting 10% reading of § 12 (Simmenthal, 106/77); reading 'appropriate' in conformity with Art 3 leads to the same result. There is no claim for hours before 1 March 2026: before the deadline only the State's duty not to seriously compromise the directive's result applies (Inter-Environnement Wallonie, C-129/96).
• Note the asymmetry with a nurse at a private hospital: the same directive helps Ben only because of who employs him, which has been criticised ever since Marshall.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU · not in the codex: Marshall I (152/84), Foster (C-188/89), Farrell (C-413/15), Fratelli Costanzo (103/88), Simmenthal (106/77), Inter-Environnement Wallonie (C-129/96).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 4(c) (case exercise, continued): Directive (EU) 2024/1690 on night work in hospitals and emergency medical services (fictional) had to be transposed by 1 March 2026. Its Art 3 obliges Member States to ensure that night workers (22:00–06:00) in hospitals or emergency medical services receive from their employer an allowance of at least 25% of their basic hourly wage for every hour of night work. Assume that the Directive is valid. Valdoria, an EU Member State, has adopted no transposition measures. § 12 of the Valdorian Working Time Act (1994) provides: 'Night work shall be compensated in an appropriate manner'; the Valdorian courts have consistently read this as 10%. Anna, a night nurse at the privately owned hospital company Medicor GmbH, sues Medicor for the difference between 10% and 25% since 1 March 2026. The labour court has found that she cannot invoke the Directive directly against her private employer. (i) What must the court nevertheless do with § 12? (ii) Would your answer change if § 12 read: 'Night work shall be compensated by an allowance of 10% of the hourly wage'? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (i) The court must read 'appropriate' in § 12 in conformity with Art 3, i.e. as at least 25%, even against settled case law. (ii) With a fixed rate of 10% that would be contra legem, so Anna would lose against Medicor and would have to claim damages from Valdoria.
• Rule (indirect effect): all national authorities, the courts included, must interpret national law as far as possible in the light of the wording and purpose of the directive (Von Colson, 14/83; Art 288(3) TFEU, Art 4(3) TEU). This applies between private parties and to law adopted before the directive (Marleasing, C-106/89). The court must consider the whole of national law and its methods of interpretation (Pfeiffer, C-397/01). The duty applies once the transposition period has expired (Adeneler, C-212/04), and the provision need not be directly effective.
• (i) 'Appropriate' is an open term, so it must be read as at least 25% from 1 March 2026. Settled case law is no obstacle: courts must change case law that is incompatible with a directive, and the employer cannot rely on legal certainty or legitimate expectations to keep it (DI, C-441/14). Anna wins the difference for her night hours since 1 March 2026.
• (ii) Limits: there can be no contra legem interpretation (Impact, C-268/06; Dominguez, C-282/10). Legal certainty and non-retroactivity also set limits, and the duty can never create or aggravate criminal liability (Kolpinghuis, 80/86). '10%' cannot mean '25%'. Nor may the court disapply § 12 on the basis of the directive in a dispute between private parties (Faccini Dori, C-91/92; Smith, C-122/17).
• Consequence in variant (ii): Anna loses against Medicor, but she can claim the difference (15 percentage points for every night hour since 1 March 2026) from Valdoria under Francovich. Art 3 confers rights on her, total non-transposition is per se a sufficiently serious breach, and it caused her loss.
Codex: Art 288(3) TFEU; Art 4(3) TEU · not in the codex: Von Colson (14/83), Marleasing (C-106/89), Pfeiffer (C-397/01), Adeneler (C-212/04), DI (C-441/14), Impact (C-268/06), Dominguez (C-282/10), Kolpinghuis (80/86), Faccini Dori (C-91/92), Smith (C-122/17), Francovich (C-6/90).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 4(d) (case exercise, continued): Directive (EU) 2024/1690 on night work in hospitals and emergency medical services (fictional) was adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure and had to be transposed by 1 March 2026. Its Art 3 obliges Member States to ensure that night workers (22:00–06:00) in hospitals or emergency medical services receive from their employer an allowance of at least 25% of their basic hourly wage for every hour of night work. Art 7: 'Member States shall ensure that, where an employer is insolvent, outstanding allowances under Article 3 are paid by a guarantee institution. Member States shall lay down the organisation and financing of that institution and may limit its liability to the allowances for the last three months before the onset of insolvency.' Assume that the Directive is valid. Valdoria, an EU Member State, has adopted no transposition measures and has set up no guarantee institution. Clara worked night shifts as a nurse at NightCare Ltd, a privately owned hospital. NightCare became insolvent on 1 September 2026 and has not paid her night allowances for June, July and August 2026; nothing can be recovered from the insolvency estate. Clara sues the Republic of Valdoria for the unpaid allowances. Advise Clara. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Not under Art 7 directly, because the directive leaves open who the guarantor is. But Clara can claim damages from Valdoria under Francovich: non-transposition is per se a sufficiently serious breach of a rule conferring rights on her, and it caused her loss.
• No direct effect: Art 7 identifies the beneficiaries and the content of the guarantee (outstanding Art 3 allowances, at least for the last three months). It does not identify the debtor, because the Member State organises and finances the guarantee institution, and the State cannot be treated as the debtor merely because it failed to transpose (Francovich, C-6/90 and C-9/90). NightCare is a private party and is insolvent anyway.
• Legal basis: State liability is inherent in the system of the Treaties (Francovich). It rests on effet utile and on Art 4(3) and 19(1) TEU. It is not Art 340(2) TFEU, which concerns the liability of the Union.
• Conditions (Brasserie du Pêcheur, C-46/93 and C-48/93): (1) The rule must be intended to confer rights: Art 7 guarantees night workers their outstanding allowances, and the beneficiaries and content can be identified. Met. (2) The breach must be sufficiently serious: a total failure to transpose by the deadline is per se serious (Dillenkofer, C-178/94). Met. (3) There must be damage and a direct causal link: with a guarantee institution, Clara would have been paid for June to August 2026, which falls within the three-month limit even if Valdoria had used that option. Met. National law may not add a further fault requirement (Brasserie).
• Procedure and amount: Clara sues Valdoria in the Valdorian courts under national liability rules, which must respect equivalence and effectiveness (Francovich; Rewe, 33/76). Compensation must be commensurate with the loss: the 25% allowances for her night hours from June to August 2026 that the guarantee institution would have paid, less anything recovered in the insolvency.
• Side note: an infringement action by the Commission (Art 258 TFEU) would not compensate Clara. As this is a failure to notify transposition of a directive adopted under a legislative procedure, a lump sum or penalty payment could already be imposed in the first judgment (Art 260(3) TFEU).
Codex: Art 4(3), 19(1) TEU; Art 258, 260(3), 288(3), 340(2) TFEU · not in the codex: Francovich (C-6/90 and C-9/90), Brasserie du Pêcheur (C-46/93 and C-48/93), Dillenkofer (C-178/94), Rewe (33/76).
